_comment: Corrections to extracted quotes, keyed by guest_slug then film_id. Quotes are generated by the LLM pass in extract_quotes.py, so an entry here contradicts it on purpose and must cite transcript evidence in its note. Set "quote" to a verbatim passage from the guest's own transcript, or to null to clear a quote that belongs to a different pick. Applied by extract_quotes.py after every run, so a re-extraction cannot silently revert the correction. Two kinds of defect qualify: the model attributed one utterance to the wrong film, or it truncated an utterance mid-thought and dropped the words that complete it. In the second case the replacement may also drop filler and asides, marking every cut with an ellipsis. The hard limit either way is that every word must be verbatim from that guest's transcript -- this file re-cuts what the guest said, it never rewrites it. NOT for polishing wording the model got right, and NOT for the ordinary case where a guest genuinely covers several films in one breath, which is legitimate and common.

roma-1972.quote: Now, Fellini. I love Amarcord, I love all his neorealism period and all that. But this movie and Casanova are the ones I revisit the most. I remember one of my favorite scenes ever committed to film, I won't ruin it for you, is the scene where they discover the frescoes in the subway. Watch it. And there are moments here where the music and the staging, the sort of fashion design for Cardinals, the way that whole set piece works is like a horror movie.
roma-1972.note: Both Roma entries -- Fellini's 1972 film and Cuaron's 2018 one -- were given the same quote, which is entirely about Cuaron's: 'Alfonso had been talking about making this movie... for about 20 years.' The transcript shows del Toro discussing Fellini's Roma from 193s, naming the frescoes in the subway and the fashion show for Cardinals, both scenes from the 1972 film, and only then saying at 227s 'Oh, I found another Roma that I like' as he moves to Cuaron's. The passage restored here is his verbatim Fellini section; the Cuaron quote stays on roma-2018.

salvatore-giuliano.note: This carried Salo's words, not its own. The transcript reads 'last time I was here it was 2009 and I said that this movie was a good date movie uh solo my favorite part of this movie is when um and then the guy he goes into a room and he finds his plate of it is not a good date movie just want to clear that up'. 'Solo' is the captioner mishearing 'Salo', and the man who goes into a room and finds his plate of excrement is Salo, not Salvatore Giuliano. The model inserted the words 'Salvatore Giuliano.' into the passage to fit the pick it was asked about. The same utterance already sits on salo-or-the-120-days-of-sodom, where it belongs, so this one is cleared.

salo-or-the-120-days-of-sodom.quote: Last time I was here it was 2009 and I said that this movie was a good date movie. Salò. My favorite part of this movie is when... and then the guy, he goes into a room and he finds his plate of... It is not a good date movie, just want to clear that up.
salo-or-the-120-days-of-sodom.note: Came from the audio fallback and shipped raw: 'Said that this movie was a good date movie solo my favorite part of this movie is when and then the guy he goes into a room...' -- opening clause missing, no punctuation, and 'solo' where the captioner misheard 'Salo'. Restored to the transcript's own wording with the sentence breaks the clean step would normally add. Nothing is added that he did not say.

the-before-trilogy.quote: The Before Trilogy. I adore all of these films made by Richard Linklater. But Before Midnight stayed with me the most because there was something about the representation of just a real marriage. And the argument at the end, which I’ve tried to recreate in other shows of mine, actually, but never could. But that argument that they have in that little hotel room, that starts off as lovemaking and just becomes the most violently brutal argument you could have as a married couple, is just an extraordinary thing. And it was quite an inspiration for Catastrophe when Rob and I were writing it.
the-before-trilogy.note: The extraction replaced the middle of her sentence with an ellipsis ("that little hotel room... Is just an extraordinary thing"), dropping the clause at 185-194s that says what the argument actually is: "that starts off as lovemaking and just becomes the most violently brutal argument you could have as a married couple". That clause is the substance of the pick -- it is the scene she says she tried to recreate in her own shows and that inspired Catastrophe, which she co-wrote with Rob Delaney -- and it is the line our October 2026 social post quoted, so the guest page has to carry it. Restored as one unbroken passage from 155s to 199s; every word is verbatim from the jAGUJQWv5kk transcript and nothing is cut.

do-the-right-thing.quote: I’m going to start with Do the Right Thing. So Spike Lee always had this thing where he said that he never ripped off directors, he paid homage to them. And I have paid homage to this film so many times in so many of my films. His more important film to me, on one level, was actually She’s Gotta Have It, because that was the very first film that I went… very first Black film that I went into a movie theater and bought popcorn and was able to buy popcorn and a soda to watch it. Normally, Black movies, you see them in a university or an educational setting, or you see it in an art house, or you see it in an art museum. This was just a straight-up movie theater. Spike Lee gave birth to so many Black filmmakers you wouldn’t believe it.
do-the-right-thing.note: The extraction dropped one word that the whole anecdote depends on. She says She’s Gotta Have It was "the very first film that I went… very first Black film that I went into a movie theater and bought popcorn" (26-36s), correcting herself mid-sentence, and then explains why that mattered: Black films were normally shown at universities, art houses or museums, and this was "a straight-up movie theater" (36-45s). The model kept the uncorrected half and cut the explanation, so the stored quote claimed it was the first film she had ever seen in a cinema. Restored as one unbroken passage from 7s to 50s; every word is verbatim from the _15L5kEGZ_s transcript and nothing is cut.

salo-or-the-120-days-of-sodom.quote: Salò, I think I… has been a massive inspiration on me. I worked with this woman, Manuela Pavesi, and it was her favorite film. I think the wedding sequence can make you fall in love with irises. A must.
salo-or-the-120-days-of-sodom.note: The extraction ran Salò's quote on through 53s and gave Barry Lyndon nothing, although Barry Lyndon is on Criterion's page for this guest. The film is never named aloud, so the transcript alone can't place it. In the video, Anderson holds Salò from 0:28 to about 0:43 (the Manuela Pavesi and irises lines) and then holds Barry Lyndon from 0:44 to 0:53, before picking up The Complete Kubrick at 0:54 with 'And then Kubrick'. 'A must.' at 44s closes Salò, the same way 'This is a must.' closes My Beautiful Laundrette at 26s. Cut Salò's quote at 'A must.'; the rest moves to barry-lyndon.

barry-lyndon.quote: Every time I talk to Luca Guadagnino, he always tells me about this film, over and over again, and he has made me look at it in a completely different way.
barry-lyndon.note: Barry Lyndon is never named aloud. Anderson holds its case from 0:44 to 0:53, between Salò and The Complete Kubrick (see the salo-or-the-120-days-of-sodom note). The video was checked two ways: Gemini read the case titles from the full-resolution video, and the YouTube storyboard thumbnails show him switch cases at about 0:42-0:44. The extraction had attached this passage to Salò.

eclipse.quote: L'Eclisse, the, the very first, next to my first movie. L'Eclisse is the one I wanted to have, that's what I came for. And, and as it is sitting next to Young Törless, it makes it even nicer. Isn't it an honor? Michelangelo, he took me to a palazzo once in Venice to watch the parade of the boats. Well, you see, L'Eclisse is really the one what I, why I came for. And isn't it magical that you come in, there hundred, hundreds of them, and the first one I see where I stop is the Eclipse? I might just as well leave right now. But I'm very, very happy with L'Eclisse and All That Jazz.
eclipse.note: The October 2026 re-extraction ended this quote before his closing line at 347-354s, 'I'm very very happy with leg clips and all that jazz' in the captions. 'Leg clips' is L'Eclisse and All That Jazz is also his pick, so the line names both films, and the previous extraction carried it here. Kept so a re-run cannot drop it again.

beau-travail.quote: Every movie I start to make, I rewatch Beau travail, and I'm ready for the next one.
beau-travail.note: Captions at 231-236s read 'every movie I start to make I I rewatch but D ey and I'm ready for the next one'; 'but D ey' is Beau Travail. Earlier extractions wrote 'The Long Day Closes' over it. The next sentence, 'I could probably watch it every day of my life', is about To Be or Not to Be: Gemini's read of the video (212-252s) has him holding To Be or Not to Be at about 240s, when he says it and 'Oh, I have it'.

all-about-eve.note: The October 2026 re-extraction gave this pick 'I could probably watch it every day of my life... Oh, I have it. It's just greedy.' Gemini's read of the video (212-252s) has him holding To Be or Not to Be at that moment, a film he already owns and did not take, so the words are not about All About Eve. Nothing else in the transcript discusses it.

matewan.note: The October 2026 re-extraction gave Matewan his whole Lone Star story as well: the audition with John Sayles, Buddy Deeds, and the call about A Time to Kill on the Lone Star set, ending 'And right next to that we have Lone Star... We already got Matewan of his.' Only the opening 'John Sayles. Yeah. Matewan.' is about Matewan; the story stays on lone-star.
